chunks.title: Python Basics
chunks.text: Hello there and welcome to the first part in this Python series

chunks.title: Python Basics
chunks.text: where we are going to write actual Python code.

chunks.title: Python Basics
chunks.text: At the moment you should have Python installed

chunks.title: Python Basics
chunks.text: and you should have access to a code editor.

chunks.title: Python Basics
chunks.text: I will be using Visual Studio Code, but any code editor is fine.

chunks.title: Python Basics
chunks.text: Choose whatever you like.

chunks.title: Python Basics
chunks.text: What we are going to learn in this video is how code is executed,

chunks.title: Python Basics
chunks.text: we are going to cover math operations and displaying text,

chunks.title: Python Basics
chunks.text: and finally we are going to get basic user input.

chunks.title: Python Basics
chunks.text: This is the screen that we finished on in the last video,

chunks.title: Python Basics
chunks.text: where we have printed the word test,

chunks.title: Python Basics
chunks.text: meaning if you are running the code again,

chunks.title: Python Basics
chunks.text: we are getting the word test.

chunks.title: Python Basics
chunks.text: That's a pretty good start, but not what I want to do for this video.

chunks.title: Python Basics
chunks.text: Instead, I want to create a new Python file.

chunks.title: Python Basics
chunks.text: This I do by going to the explorer on the left side.

chunks.title: Python Basics
chunks.text: If you can't see it, it's this symbol. Just click on it.

chunks.title: Python Basics
chunks.text: And then right click on this area and create a new file.

chunks.title: Python Basics
chunks.text: This now needs a name and I want to call it basics.py.

chunks.title: Python Basics
chunks.text: Really important, you need the .py ending.

chunks.title: Python Basics
chunks.text: Only because of that does Visual Studio Code know

chunks.title: Python Basics
chunks.text: that we are working with a Python file.

chunks.title: Python Basics
chunks.text: If you now press enter, we have a new Python file.

chunks.title: Python Basics
chunks.text: On top of that, if you open the folder where we are working in,

chunks.title: Python Basics
chunks.text: besides setup, we now also have basics.py.

chunks.title: Python Basics
chunks.text: This is the file we just created.

chunks.title: Python Basics
chunks.text: With that, I can go into full screen,

chunks.title: Python Basics
chunks.text: so we have fewer distractions.

chunks.title: Python Basics
chunks.text: Now, just to test that this file is working,

chunks.title: Python Basics
chunks.text: let me print, let's say line 1.

chunks.title: Python Basics
chunks.text: If I run the code again, which I can do either by going on this triangle,

chunks.title: Python Basics
chunks.text: or in my case, I can use the custom hotkey alt and a,

chunks.title: Python Basics
chunks.text: that is doing the same thing. I set this one up in the last video.

chunks.title: Python Basics
chunks.text: If we are doing that, we are getting the output line 1.

chunks.title: Python Basics
chunks.text: And all of this is getting a bit messy.

chunks.title: Python Basics
chunks.text: If you want to clean it up, you can go to these three dots and then clear terminal.

chunks.title: Python Basics
chunks.text: That way things are a bit cleaner.

chunks.title: Python Basics
chunks.text: And if you run it again, you get a bit less clutter.

chunks.title: Python Basics
chunks.text: It's not ideal, but it's good enough.

chunks.title: Python Basics
chunks.text: The thing we care about is line 1.

chunks.title: Python Basics
chunks.text: So we know this Python code is working.

chunks.title: Python Basics
chunks.text: Well, that's a good sign.

chunks.title: Python Basics
chunks.text: Which is bringing us to the first fundamental concept.

chunks.title: Python Basics
chunks.text: Code in Python and basically any programming language is always executed from the top,

chunks.title: Python Basics
chunks.text: meaning line 1, and then we are going down.

chunks.title: Python Basics
chunks.text: For example, if we have more than one line,

chunks.title: Python Basics
chunks.text: we have line 1, line 2, and line 3.

chunks.title: Python Basics
chunks.text: We always start with line 1, then we execute the second print statement,

chunks.title: Python Basics
chunks.text: and then we execute the third print statement.

chunks.title: Python Basics
chunks.text: Which means if I run the code now,

chunks.title: Python Basics
chunks.text: we can see line 1, line 2, and line 3 in this order.

chunks.title: Python Basics
chunks.text: Later on, we are going to learn how to manipulate this order.

chunks.title: Python Basics
chunks.text: For example, to create a loop where code runs forever,

chunks.title: Python Basics
chunks.text: or the ability to only run code if a certain condition is true.

chunks.title: Python Basics
chunks.text: But for now, we always run code from the start to the end.

chunks.title: Python Basics
chunks.text: Like you would read any book.

chunks.title: Python Basics
chunks.text: I think that makes sense.

chunks.title: Python Basics
chunks.text: Also, what you can do to organize a code a bit better is to add comments,

chunks.title: Python Basics
chunks.text: which you do with the hashtag symbol.

chunks.title: Python Basics
chunks.text: Anything after that will be ignored by Python.

chunks.title: Python Basics
chunks.text: Let's call this one the execution order.

chunks.title: Python Basics
chunks.text: You can also write a comment after a line of code.

chunks.title: Python Basics
chunks.text: All you have to do is add the hashtag,

chunks.title: Python Basics
chunks.text: and anything after that will be ignored.

chunks.title: Python Basics
chunks.text: So this will be ignored.

chunks.title: Python Basics
chunks.text: Super handy to add some annotations to certain lines of code,

chunks.title: Python Basics
chunks.text: or to entire blocks.

chunks.title: Python Basics
chunks.text: Cool. With that, we have the first important concept.

chunks.title: Python Basics
chunks.text: The next important concept would be data types,

chunks.title: Python Basics
chunks.text: because in Python, we have multiple.

chunks.title: Python Basics
chunks.text: The one we have already seen, let me print it again,

chunks.title: Python Basics
chunks.text: is simply words.

chunks.title: Python Basics
chunks.text: So let's call it words.

chunks.title: Python Basics
chunks.text: This could either be done with single quotation marks,

chunks.title: Python Basics
chunks.text: or with double quotation marks.

chunks.title: Python Basics
chunks.text: Meaning if I print double quotation mark words,

chunks.title: Python Basics
chunks.text: we would get the same result.

chunks.title: Python Basics
chunks.text: If I run the code again, we get words two times.

chunks.title: Python Basics
chunks.text: One with single quotation marks, and one with double quotation marks.

chunks.title: Python Basics
chunks.text: Python doesn't really care.

chunks.title: Python Basics
chunks.text: You just have to be consistent.

chunks.title: Python Basics
chunks.text: Besides that, the other data type would be numbers.

chunks.title: Python Basics
chunks.text: For example, we could print 1, 2, 3.

chunks.title: Python Basics
chunks.text: We could print negative 10,

chunks.title: Python Basics
chunks.text: or we could print 1.5.

chunks.title: Python Basics
chunks.text: I can run all of this again, and we're getting words,

chunks.title: Python Basics
chunks.text: and then the numbers that we have just specified.

chunks.title: Python Basics
chunks.text: These values are created via different data types.

chunks.title: Python Basics
chunks.text: Words in Python are called strings.

chunks.title: Python Basics
chunks.text: And those you create either with single, or with double quotation marks.

chunks.title: Python Basics
chunks.text: Both would be fine.

chunks.title: Python Basics
chunks.text: Numbers can be integers, or ints in short,

chunks.title: Python Basics
chunks.text: and those could be either positive or negative.

chunks.title: Python Basics
chunks.text: And if a number has a decimal point,

chunks.title: Python Basics
chunks.text: it is called a floating point value,

chunks.title: Python Basics
chunks.text: or simply a float.

chunks.title: Python Basics
chunks.text: Internally, Python is processing these numbers

chunks.title: Python Basics
chunks.text: slightly differently compared to the integers.

chunks.title: Python Basics
chunks.text: But that's not something you have to worry about.

chunks.title: Python Basics
chunks.text: What you do have to worry about, however,

chunks.title: Python Basics
chunks.text: are basic, let's call it operations.

chunks.title: Python Basics
chunks.text: For example, what you could be doing

chunks.title: Python Basics
chunks.text: is print, let's say, 3 plus 3.

chunks.title: Python Basics
chunks.text: Also, what you can do with comments,

chunks.title: Python Basics
chunks.text: is you can select all of this,

chunks.title: Python Basics
chunks.text: and then press ctrl and a forward slash.

chunks.title: Python Basics
chunks.text: That way, you comment out all of the selected lines of code.

chunks.title: Python Basics
chunks.text: If you press the same combination again, you uncomment them.

chunks.title: Python Basics
chunks.text: In our case, we're going to print 3 plus 3.

chunks.title: Python Basics
chunks.text: If I now run the code again, we're getting 6.

chunks.title: Python Basics
chunks.text: And once again, let me clear the terminal,

chunks.title: Python Basics
chunks.text: so we can focus on what's happening here.

chunks.title: Python Basics
chunks.text: We are just getting 6.

chunks.title: Python Basics
chunks.text: The result of 3 plus 3.

chunks.title: Python Basics
chunks.text: That should make sense.

chunks.title: Python Basics
chunks.text: There are multiple math operations you can work with in Python.

chunks.title: Python Basics
chunks.text: In my case, I want to duplicate this line,

chunks.title: Python Basics
chunks.text: which you can do with alt, shift, and then the down arrow.

chunks.title: Python Basics
chunks.text: That way, you duplicate the line downwards.

chunks.title: Python Basics
chunks.text: The basic math operations are plus, minus, multiply, and divide.

chunks.title: Python Basics
chunks.text: If I now run all of this, we get 6, 0, 9, and 1.0.

chunks.title: Python Basics
chunks.text: The respective results of these 4 operations.

chunks.title: Python Basics
chunks.text: Notice here that whenever you divide a value in Python,

chunks.title: Python Basics
chunks.text: the result will be a floating point value.

chunks.title: Python Basics
chunks.text: Which is interesting, but not something you have to be concerned about.

chunks.title: Python Basics
chunks.text: Because you can add these values up totally fine.

chunks.title: Python Basics
chunks.text: For example, we could do 10 plus 0.

chunks.title: Python Basics
chunks.text: some longer floating point value.

chunks.title: Python Basics
chunks.text: If I now add them together, we get the expected result.

chunks.title: Python Basics
chunks.text: So integers and floating point values can be added together perfectly fine.

chunks.title: Python Basics
chunks.text: What cannot be added together would be integers or floating point values and strings.

chunks.title: Python Basics
chunks.text: And this should make sense.

chunks.title: Python Basics
chunks.text: Imagine somebody asked you to add together 10 and the word hello.

chunks.title: Python Basics
chunks.text: You wouldn't have any idea what to do with that.

chunks.title: Python Basics
chunks.text: And Python is in the same spot.

chunks.title: Python Basics
chunks.text: If I try to run the code, we are getting an error message.

chunks.title: Python Basics
chunks.text: That we have a type error, unsupported operand type for plus, int, and string.

chunks.title: Python Basics
chunks.text: Python just doesn't know what to do with this operation.

chunks.title: Python Basics
chunks.text: And for good reason. It doesn't make any sense.

chunks.title: Python Basics
chunks.text: What you could be doing, however, is 10 multiplied with hello.

chunks.title: Python Basics
chunks.text: And the result of that is going to be the string hello 10 times.

chunks.title: Python Basics
chunks.text: This isn't something you usually do, but in very rare circumstances, this can be useful.

chunks.title: Python Basics
chunks.text: What I want you guys to focus on is that sometimes you can add different data types together very easily.

chunks.title: Python Basics
chunks.text: Like integers and floating point values.

chunks.title: Python Basics
chunks.text: But other times this is not possible.

chunks.title: Python Basics
chunks.text: For example, multiplying an integer with a string is a bit weird, but doable.

chunks.title: Python Basics
chunks.text: But you can't add them together.

chunks.title: Python Basics
chunks.text: There aren't really that many rules.

chunks.title: Python Basics
chunks.text: Most of the time, the expected result is what you would be getting.

chunks.title: Python Basics
chunks.text: Speaking of which, there's one more thing I want to cover.

chunks.title: Python Basics
chunks.text: And that is the order of operation.

chunks.title: Python Basics
chunks.text: Let's say we have an operation like 13 minus 3 times 4 plus 2.

chunks.title: Python Basics
chunks.text: What do you think the result is going to be from all of this?

chunks.title: Python Basics
chunks.text: Well, let's run the code and the result is going to be 3.

chunks.title: Python Basics
chunks.text: The correct order of operation is that you always start with multiplication,

chunks.title: Python Basics
chunks.text: meaning 3 times 4 would be 12.

chunks.title: Python Basics
chunks.text: After that, we can do 13 minus 12 plus 2.

chunks.title: Python Basics
chunks.text: And that's quite easy. This would simply be 3.

chunks.title: Python Basics
chunks.text: The result we have gotten down there.

chunks.title: Python Basics
chunks.text: But sometimes you do want to be a bit more specific.

chunks.title: Python Basics
chunks.text: For example, you might want this 4 plus 2 to be prioritized.

chunks.title: Python Basics
chunks.text: For that, you can use parentheses and put them in there.

chunks.title: Python Basics
chunks.text: If I now run this again, we are getting minus 5.

chunks.title: Python Basics
chunks.text: We are getting this because we start with the parentheses operation.

chunks.title: Python Basics
chunks.text: This would be 4 plus 2 or 6, which we are multiplying with 3.

chunks.title: Python Basics
chunks.text: This would give us 18.

chunks.title: Python Basics
chunks.text: And then the final calculation would be 13 minus 18, which is negative 5.

chunks.title: Python Basics
chunks.text: Exactly what we have gotten down there.

chunks.title: Python Basics
chunks.text: That should be reasonably straightforward.

chunks.title: Python Basics
chunks.text: So next up, we can cover variables.

chunks.title: Python Basics
chunks.text: And what variables allow you to do is to work over multiple lines.

chunks.title: Python Basics
chunks.text: At the moment, we are always constrained to a single line of code.

chunks.title: Python Basics
chunks.text: We can do this one, this one or this one.

chunks.title: Python Basics
chunks.text: But we couldn't connect this line to this line or this line to this line.

chunks.title: Python Basics
chunks.text: For that, we always need a variable.

chunks.title: Python Basics
chunks.text: And a variable is just a bucket where you can put a value into

chunks.title: Python Basics
chunks.text: and take a value out or change the value and do stuff like that.

chunks.title: Python Basics
chunks.text: Let's say I want to create a variable called test,

chunks.title: Python Basics
chunks.text: which you do by simply writing test.

chunks.title: Python Basics
chunks.text: And then to assign it a value, you will need the equal sign.

chunks.title: Python Basics
chunks.text: For example, in this case, I want to give it the value 1, 2 and 3.

chunks.title: Python Basics
chunks.text: We have created a variable with the value 123.

chunks.title: Python Basics
chunks.text: This we can then use.

chunks.title: Python Basics
chunks.text: For example, we could print it.

chunks.title: Python Basics
chunks.text: And if I run all of this again, we are getting 1, 2 and 3.

chunks.title: Python Basics
chunks.text: To Python, this test is simply the value of 120 and 3.

chunks.title: Python Basics
chunks.text: Which means you could even use this in math operations.

chunks.title: Python Basics
chunks.text: Let's say plus 10, run all of this again.

chunks.title: Python Basics
chunks.text: And we're getting 133.

chunks.title: Python Basics
chunks.text: 123 plus 10.

chunks.title: Python Basics
chunks.text: With that setup, you can connect multiple lines.

chunks.title: Python Basics
chunks.text: For example, what you could be doing is test is the same value,

chunks.title: Python Basics
chunks.text: except we are adding 50 to it.

chunks.title: Python Basics
chunks.text: And then we simply want to print the output.

chunks.title: Python Basics
chunks.text: Run all of this again.

chunks.title: Python Basics
chunks.text: And we're getting 173.

chunks.title: Python Basics
chunks.text: On line 23, we're creating a test variable with the value 123.

chunks.title: Python Basics
chunks.text: On the next line, we got the same variable and assigned it a new value with this equal operator.

chunks.title: Python Basics
chunks.text: After that, we got the value of the variable itself and then added 50.

chunks.title: Python Basics
chunks.text: The result was 173.

chunks.title: Python Basics
chunks.text: Now, this line isn't particularly elegant and Python has a shortcut for that.

chunks.title: Python Basics
chunks.text: What we can do is plus equal 50.

chunks.title: Python Basics
chunks.text: That way we are taking the same variable and adding a value to it.

chunks.title: Python Basics
chunks.text: So if I now run all of this again, we are still getting 173.

chunks.title: Python Basics
chunks.text: Variables are incredibly useful and we are going to use them all the time.

chunks.title: Python Basics
chunks.text: Although when using them, you do have to be careful

chunks.title: Python Basics
chunks.text: because there are some limitations on the name you can use.

chunks.title: Python Basics
chunks.text: Let's talk about that.

chunks.title: Python Basics
chunks.text: When it comes to variable names, there are some parts that are mandatory.

chunks.title: Python Basics
chunks.text: If you're not doing them, you are going to get an error message.

chunks.title: Python Basics
chunks.text: Most importantly, you can only use the letters from A to Z,

chunks.title: Python Basics
chunks.text: both lowercase and uppercase, the numbers 0 to 9 and the underscore symbol.

chunks.title: Python Basics
chunks.text: These are the only characters that are allowed.

chunks.title: Python Basics
chunks.text: Besides that, we cannot start with a number,

chunks.title: Python Basics
chunks.text: meaning one test would be invalid, but test1 would be fine.

chunks.title: Python Basics
chunks.text: After that, variable names are case sensitive.

chunks.title: Python Basics
chunks.text: So test123 would be different from test123

chunks.title: Python Basics
chunks.text: because the first one has a lowercase t while the second one has an uppercase t.

chunks.title: Python Basics
chunks.text: As far as Python is concerned, those are two entirely separate variables.

chunks.title: Python Basics
chunks.text: Finally, the last limitation is that we cannot use the names of inbuilt functions.

chunks.title: Python Basics
chunks.text: So for example, print couldn't be a variable name.

chunks.title: Python Basics
chunks.text: That would be really confusing.

chunks.title: Python Basics
chunks.text: After that, there are a couple of things that are beneficial, but not mandatory.

chunks.title: Python Basics
chunks.text: The first one is that you should be clear with your variable names.

chunks.title: Python Basics
chunks.text: For example, you could create a value that is called a

chunks.title: Python Basics
chunks.text: and assign it a value of, let's say, 150.

chunks.title: Python Basics
chunks.text: This a has no inherent meaning.

chunks.title: Python Basics
chunks.text: If somebody else was to look at it, they would have no idea what you are trying to do.

chunks.title: Python Basics
chunks.text: Also, when you are not looking at this code for half a year and come back to it,

chunks.title: Python Basics
chunks.text: you will yourself have no idea what this a stands for.

chunks.title: Python Basics
chunks.text: So you shouldn't use this kind of a at all.

chunks.title: Python Basics
chunks.text: It should be something more descriptive.

chunks.title: Python Basics
chunks.text: Depends on your use case, but you should rather have longer than shorter variable names.

chunks.title: Python Basics
chunks.text: After that, you should also use what is called snake case.

chunks.title: Python Basics
chunks.text: What this one means is that every character is always lowercase.

chunks.title: Python Basics
chunks.text: And if you want to separate two words as one variable name,

chunks.title: Python Basics
chunks.text: you are separating them with an underscore.

chunks.title: Python Basics
chunks.text: Back in the code, this test, we could call, for example, test value.

chunks.title: Python Basics
chunks.text: And since this name changed, we have to change the name of all of the other test variables as well,

chunks.title: Python Basics
chunks.text: so we stay consistent.

chunks.title: Python Basics
chunks.text: If I now run this again, we get the same outcome.

chunks.title: Python Basics
chunks.text: So test value is perfectly fine.

chunks.title: Python Basics
chunks.text: Still not an amazing name for a variable, but it will do for now.

chunks.title: Python Basics
chunks.text: What you couldn't be doing, however, is add a number at the beginning.

chunks.title: Python Basics
chunks.text: That way, you immediately get a scary red color, so you can see this one isn't working.

chunks.title: Python Basics
chunks.text: You also wouldn't be allowed to use other characters,

chunks.title: Python Basics
chunks.text: like, for example, a pound sign.

chunks.title: Python Basics
chunks.text: There you can see we get an error message right away.

chunks.title: Python Basics
chunks.text: Also, what is not allowed to have is space between these values.

chunks.title: Python Basics
chunks.text: There you can see right away we get lots of error messages, so let's not do that.

chunks.title: Python Basics
chunks.text: Creating variable names will eventually become quite straightforward,

chunks.title: Python Basics
chunks.text: and you develop an intuition for it.

chunks.title: Python Basics
chunks.text: For now, don't worry too much about it.

chunks.title: Python Basics
chunks.text: As long as you don't get an error message, the variable name is going to be fine.

chunks.title: Python Basics
chunks.text: Which means now we can come to the last part of this video,

chunks.title: Python Basics
chunks.text: and that is getting input.

chunks.title: Python Basics
chunks.text: And for all of that, I want to comment out the earlier parts,

chunks.title: Python Basics
chunks.text: so we can focus on one thing at a time.

chunks.title: Python Basics
chunks.text: To get input, you will need a function that works kind of like the print statement.

chunks.title: Python Basics
chunks.text: It is called input.

chunks.title: Python Basics
chunks.text: This one, like print, wants to have a string that it is going to display.

chunks.title: Python Basics
chunks.text: For example, we could write,

chunks.title: Python Basics
chunks.text: please write something.

chunks.title: Python Basics
chunks.text: If I now run the code, and let me clear the terminal once again,

chunks.title: Python Basics
chunks.text: there we get, please write something, with a square afterwards.

chunks.title: Python Basics
chunks.text: And there we can actually type something.

chunks.title: Python Basics
chunks.text: So, e, word, and if I now press enter,

chunks.title: Python Basics
chunks.text: we are finishing the code.

chunks.title: Python Basics
chunks.text: So what happened?

chunks.title: Python Basics
chunks.text: Well, when you are running this kind of command,

chunks.title: Python Basics
chunks.text: Python is going to display the text, and then check for user input.

chunks.title: Python Basics
chunks.text: Which in our case is working totally fine.

chunks.title: Python Basics
chunks.text: The issue is, we are not storing the value, or do anything with it.

chunks.title: Python Basics
chunks.text: For that though, we can use a variable.

chunks.title: Python Basics
chunks.text: For example, we could assign this value to a variable called user input.

chunks.title: Python Basics
chunks.text: And then on the next line, we could print that user input.

chunks.title: Python Basics
chunks.text: Also what I want to do, is to add a space after something,

chunks.title: Python Basics
chunks.text: still inside of the quotation marks.

chunks.title: Python Basics
chunks.text: What that is going to do, if I run the code again,

chunks.title: Python Basics
chunks.text: we are still getting the same, please write something.

chunks.title: Python Basics
chunks.text: But now, after that, and the input square,

chunks.title: Python Basics
chunks.text: we are getting one line of a separation.

chunks.title: Python Basics
chunks.text: This is the space we have just created.

chunks.title: Python Basics
chunks.text: Looks a bit cleaner, but isn't too important.

chunks.title: Python Basics
chunks.text: What is much more important, is that now we can write any kind of value.

chunks.title: Python Basics
